process: D20: two blind graders (D7), adjudicator on disagreements, agent audit of agreed verdicts (D11)
rate_withheld: D31: top risks publish a materialised share (a calibration measure, not a hit rate) and red herrings a hit rate; the two never merge. See summary-d31.json.

verdicts.reason: The source text defines the scope: it names Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and the UAE and lists 'violence in Iraq, Iran' as surrounding concerns, not as the Gulf whose stability is forecast. On that reading B is right: the GCC states stayed stable and Dubai's debt standstill was contained by Abu Dhabi, as the text itself anticipated. Grader A's reading error: it counted Iran's post-election protests, which the source places outside the claim; the Saudi-Houthi border operation was a military action, not political instability in the Gulf states.

The source's mechanism is rising attacks on Indian targets that push Delhi to a tougher line on Pakistan. One such attack happened (Pune German Bakery bombing, Feb 2010, 17-18 dead) and Kashmir unrest was severe, but there was no large-scale attack and no escalation: foreign-secretary and ministerial talks continued. Occurred in part (smaller scale). Grader B graded a stricter 'materially escalates' reading and ignored the Pune attack, which is the mechanism the source names.

The source names Ukraine, Hungary and Latvia as most vulnerable. Hungary materialised fully: Fidesz won a two-thirds majority, imposed bank taxes, broke off IMF review talks (July 2010) and nationalised private pension assets. Ukraine elected Yanukovych but signed a new IMF stand-by in July 2010; Latvia re-elected its austerity government in Oct 2010; Poland saw no such stress. Only some named countries: partial under D31. Grader A's Romania example is not among the named countries.

The core channels the source names (G20 economic coordination, current-account imbalances, climate) all failed in 2011: Cannes G20 made little progress, the Doha deadline was missed, Durban deferred a binding deal, the US debt-ceiling fight absorbed Washington. Libya (UNSC 1973) is a single exception on security, not on the economic-governance channel the entry centres on. The development happened with documented effect: hit. Grader B's facts are correct but one exception does not make the risk smaller in scale.

Several countries imposed new controls in 2011: Brazil extended the IOF to foreign borrowing under 360 days (28 Mar) then 720 days (early Apr) and added a currency-derivatives tax (Jul); Korea reinstated a bond withholding tax (Jan) and levied up to 0.2% on banks' foreign debt from Aug. Grader B's chronology omits Brazil's March-April loan IOF and leans on the Jan equity cut and Dec rollback; the Dec reversal came after the inflow phase and does not undo the year's new controls.

The source anticipated a tense north-south election, persisting sectarian clashes and a Jonathan win, and forecast only that politics would not be fundamentally unstable. That is what happened: Jonathan won in April 2011, the result held and the constitutional order survived. The post-election violence (~800 dead) and Boko Haram attacks are serious but fall within the messiness the claim allowed; no systemic breakdown. Grader A counted anticipated messiness as partial materialisation of the feared risk.

The source centres on regime instability ('history's first leaderless nuclear power', collapse bringing US and Chinese troops face to face). No implosion: Kim Jong Un consolidated power. Provocation occurred only in a routine, smaller form: two satellite launches (13 Apr failed, 12 Dec orbit) condemned under UN resolutions; no nuclear test, no attack on the South. Smaller scale: partial. Grader A treated any launch as the full 'explosion' branch.

Domestic turmoil was real (PM Gilani convicted April, disqualified June 2012 by the Supreme Court) but there was no military interference, and the spillover channels the source stresses (Taliban safe havens after US drawdown, India-Pakistan proxy war in Afghanistan) did not produce a new crisis. The NATO supply-route closure was a 2011 carry-over that ended in July 2012. Some channels only: partial. Grader A's hit rests on the supply closure, which began in Nov 2011 and is not the spillover the source describes.

The source forecasts rising economic populism and a negative trajectory, not a single crisis. Both came with documented effect in 2013: Malema launched the EFF on a nationalisation and expropriation platform (Jul 2013), mining labour conflict continued, the Nkandla scandal grew, and South Africa was named one of the 'Fragile Five' as the rand weakened. Grader B required a crisis-scale shock, which the claim does not state.

The source's forecast is that the feared protectionist turn does not come and that competitive liberalisation (TPP, a transatlantic deal) quickens. TTIP negotiations opened in July 2013, TPP talks continued and the WTO concluded the Bali Package in Dec 2013. WTO G-20 monitoring shows only a slow creep in restrictive measures (116 vs 109). Grader B's Global Trade Alert count covers June 2012 to May 2013, mostly before the edition year, and counts low-visibility measures rather than the systemic rise the red herring addresses.

All six elections happened and outcomes diverged as forecast: India's BJP won the first single-party majority since 1984 and markets rallied; Indonesia elected Jokowi; Colombia re-elected Santos (the source's positive case) and peace talks continued; Brazil re-elected Rousseff by 51.6% into recession; Turkey's Erdogan consolidated. Grader B treated unevenness as partial, but uneven outcomes are the divergence the claim forecasts.

The source explicitly carves out Venezuela ('the one exception ... very real threat of near-term instability'). Russia, Saudi Arabia and the smaller Gulf producers stayed stable in 2015. Grader A's reading error: it graded the Venezuelan opposition's Dec 2015 assembly win against the red herring, though the source placed Venezuela outside it.

The source centres on ISIS's reach and names the states it expects to be hit. ISIS-attributed deaths rose 49% in 2016 (GTI 2017) and major attacks struck named targets: Brussels (Mar), Orlando (Jun), Istanbul airport (Jun), Baghdad Karrada (Jul), Nice (Jul), Berlin (Dec); 77 countries recorded a terrorism death, the most in 17 years. Total terrorism deaths fell 13%, driven by Boko Haram and Afghanistan/Pakistan, which the source does not list as vulnerable targets. Grader A weighted the aggregate death count over the ISIS channel the entry is about.

The source names Trump revoking waivers and ending sanctions relief as a path to the deal's failure. That happened: US withdrawal on 8 May 2018, sanctions reimposed in Aug and Nov, Iran's currency and oil exports collapsed, and the EU invoked its blocking statute. The development in the summary happened with documented effect in 2018. Grader A required Iran's exit and military escalation; the source lists US withdrawal as sufficient for failure, and the later 2019 escalation is beyond the year but not required for a hit.

The source explicitly allowed for 'an outright radical euroskeptic' Italian government and forecast only that the economy would not fall apart and Italy would not leave. That is what happened: the Conte government clashed with the Commission over its budget, settled in December; Germany formed its coalition in March; euro-area growth was 1.8%. Grader A counted the anticipated Italian clash as partial materialisation.

The quote places the fruit 'in years to come', so the reading 'dangers bear fruit in 2019' is not a faithful in-year reading; the faithful in-year reading is that the named dynamics keep deteriorating. That is documented: the US left the INF Treaty (2 Aug 2019), the WTO Appellate Body lost its quorum (11 Dec 2019), US-China tariffs escalated (May, Sep 2019), and Macron called NATO 'brain dead' (Nov 2019). One reading dominates, so not unfalsifiable; the named institutions are observable, so not ungradable. Both graders declined to grade; low certainty.

The source's named outcomes: record euroskeptic seats (partly: ID 73, up from 36), second-largest group (no: EPP, S&D, Renew and Greens were larger), populist commissioners shaping the Commission (no: Parliament rejected Hungary's nominee Trocsanyi), populist governments holding (no: FPÖ left Austria's government after Ibiza in May, Lega left Italy's in August). Smaller scale and only some channels: partial. Grader B graded the seat gain and did not test the power claims the source makes.

The source forecasts a close vote with a possibly challenged or inconclusive result. The vote was disrupted (postponed a week at 03:00 on polling day, violence, supplementary polls) and Atiku challenged it to the Supreme Court, but it was not close: Buhari won 55.6% to 41.2%, a wider margin than 2015's 54-45, so 'most fiercely contested since 1999' is not borne out by the result. Some channels only: partial. Grader B graded disruption and the court challenge without testing the closeness the source names.

The source names three channels. Sectarian instability happened with documented effect (Delhi riots, Feb 2020, 53 dead; continued anti-CAA protests). The foreign-policy channel did not: US-India ties deepened (Trump visit Feb 2020, BECA signed Oct 2020) and no CAATSA sanctions came in 2020. The economic channel cannot be separated from the COVID contraction. Only some channels: partial under D31. Grader B graded the social channel alone.

The report was published 6 Jan 2020, after the Soleimani killing, and explicitly expected Iranian retaliation 'probably even direct strikes against the US and allies' while betting against war; for North Korea it expected missile provocations short of the brink. Iran's 8 Jan missile strike on US bases was the anticipated retaliation and was followed by de-escalation; no war with any of the three. Grader B's reading error: it counted the Soleimani killing (before publication) and the anticipated retaliation as partial materialisation.

The source predicted headline commitments ('climate commitments will matter in 2021 like never before') and, beneath them, competition. The named mechanisms occurred: the EU proposed CBAM (14 Jul 2021); India and China forced the coal 'phase-down' wording at COP26; NDCs fell well short of 1.5C; US-China clean-tech rivalry intensified. Grader B counted the Glasgow Pact and US-China declaration as coordination against the claim, but the source anticipated exactly such headline pledges.

Graders read 'foreign adventures' from the edition summary, but the quote says only 'misadventures', and the Top Risks 2021 PDF (pp. 15-16) names premature monetary easing and rate cuts as the first step. en.wikipedia Turkish economic crisis: governor fired, rates cut 19% to 14%, lira -44% in 2021. The stated development occurred in full.

The source's named outcomes mostly happened: a severe early-2021 wave before vaccines (Peru highest COVID death rate in the world), Fernandez weakened in Argentina's midterms, Morena kept its Mexican majority, an outsider (Castillo) won in Peru, the leftist Boric won in Chile, mass unrest in Colombia. Ecuador went the other way (Lasso won). The 6.2% GDP rebound followed a 6.8% contraction and is not what the entry forecast. Grader A weighted the GDP rebound over the political channels the entry names.

The source's own text sets 'no crisis' as part of the forecast and names channels. Some happened: Republicans took the House (222-213); some losing denier candidates (e.g. Kari Lake) refused to concede and sued; Cochise County briefly refused to certify. Others did not: Democrats held the Senate, most denier candidates for state election offices lost and conceded, certification was routine overall. In part: partial. Grader A read the claim as the tipping point failing entirely and ignored the GOP House win the source forecast.

The recorded quote is a probability statement ('chance of regime collapse is low, but higher than in four decades'); non-collapse does not falsify it. Top Risks 2023 PDF p.12 frames the risk as new confrontations between Iran and the West, which graders did not check; Wikipedia Mahsa Amini protests (subsided by spring 2023) only tests a reading the source calls unlikely.

The price premise failed: Brent averaged $82.49 in 2023, down from $100.93, and did not end the year above $100. The friction channel occurred in part: the surprise OPEC+ cut (Apr 2023) and Saudi voluntary cuts (Jul 2023) drew US criticism, though US-Saudi ties did not rupture. Only one channel, at smaller scale: partial. Grader A graded the price premise alone; both graders' price figures agree with EIA.

The page both graders cite (en.wikipedia Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis) dates the crisis 2 Aug 2022 to present and records 'Joint Sword' encirclement drills 8-10 Apr 2023 with ~71 aircraft across the median line and live fire. Smaller than 2022 but not calm; it materialised in part, consistent with 2023-014.
